- **Akaike information criterion (AIC)**: A criterion to compare models fitted to the same
data, calculated as
$$
\mathrm{AIC} = 2K - 2\,\ell(\hat\theta),
$$
where $\ell(\hat\theta)$ is the maximum log-likelihood of the model and $K$ is the number of
parameters that were estimated. Among models fitted to the same observations, the one with
the lowest AIC is preferred, and only differences in AIC are meaningful. AIC ranks the
candidate models: it does not tell us whether the best of them describes the data well.

- **Aleatoric probability**: Probability interpreted as the relative frequency at which
different values would be observed across all the possible replications of the same
experiment or observation protocol. It relates to measurement error and to stochasticity
and variability in ecological systems. This is the interpretation of probability used in
this course.

- **Asymptote**: A line that the graph of a function approaches. A
horizontal asymptote is a finite limit of the function as $x\to\infty$ (or $-\infty$). The
upper asymptote $a$ of the Michaelis–Menten function $ax/(b+x)$ is an example.

- **Asymptotic efficiency**: An estimator is asymptotically efficient when, in large samples,
its variance is as small as the Cramér–Rao bound allows, so that no other regular estimator
is more precise. Maximum likelihood estimators have this property under regularity
conditions.

- **Asymptotically normal**: An estimator is asymptotically normal when its sampling
distribution approaches a Normal distribution as the sample size grows. For the mean of
i.i.d. observations from a distribution with finite variance, this follows from the central
limit theorem. The maximum likelihood estimator of any parameter is asymptotically normal
under regularity conditions, centred on the parameter and with a variance equal to the
inverse of the Fisher information.

- **Bandwidth**: The standard deviation of the kernel used in a kernel density estimate. It
plays the same role as the bin width of a histogram: a small bandwidth gives a wiggly
estimate and a large bandwidth a very smooth one.

- **Bias**: The difference between the mean of the sampling distribution of an estimator
and the parameter that it estimates,
$$
\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta) = E[\hat\theta] - \theta.
$$
An estimator is **unbiased** when its bias is zero. Bias is a property of the whole
sampling distribution: individual estimates of an unbiased estimator still fall above or
below the parameter.

- **Central limit theorem**: The mean of $n$ i.i.d. observations from a distribution with
finite variance has a sampling distribution that approaches a Normal distribution as $n$
grows, regardless of the distribution of the individual observations.

- **Central moment**: An expectation used to describe features of a distribution. The $k$th
central moment is $E[(X-E[X])^k]$. Variance is the central moment for $k = 2$. Skewness and kurtosis are calculated from the
central moments for $k = 3$ and $k = 4$.

- **Characteristic scale**: The distance along the $x$ axis over which a function changes by a
fixed proportion. It is the value of a scale parameter that divides $x$, or the inverse of
one that multiplies $x$. For the exponential decay $ae^{-bx}$ it is $1/b$, the distance over
which the function falls by a factor $e$.

- **Composition**: The application of one function to the output of another, $f(x)=g(h(x))$,
where $h$ is the inner function and $g$ the outer function. It is used to give a function
the range that a quantity requires, for example $e^{a+bx}$ for a positive mean or the
inverse logit of $a+bx$ for a probability.

- **Concave and convex**: A function is concave where its second derivative is negative,
so that the graph bends downwards and the slope decreases as $x$ increases. It is convex
where the second derivative is positive, so that the graph bends upwards and the slope
increases. The Michaelis–Menten function is concave for all $x\ge0$.

- **Confidence interval**: A range of values for a parameter, calculated from a sample with
a procedure that has a known behaviour across repeated hypothetical experiments. Once an
interval has been calculated, it either contains the parameter or it does not, so the
confidence level is a property of the procedure and not a probability that the parameter
lies in that particular interval.

- **Confidence level**: The fraction of repeated hypothetical experiments for which a
confidence interval calculated with a given procedure would contain the parameter (e.g.,
95%). The actual fraction, the coverage, may differ from the intended level when the
procedure relies on approximations.

- **Consistency**: An estimator $\hat\theta_n$ calculated from a sample of size $n$ is
consistent if it converges in probability to the parameter $\theta$, that is, for any
positive margin $\varepsilon$,
$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} P\left(\left|\hat\theta_n - \theta\right| \ge \varepsilon\right)=0.
$$
It describes the probability of large errors, not the ordering of the estimates of two
particular samples.

- **Continuous random variable**: A random variable that can take any value within an
interval of the real numbers (e.g., all positive numbers, or all numbers between 0 and 1).
Its values cannot be listed one by one, the probability of any single value is zero, and
its distribution assigns probabilities to intervals through a probability density function.

- **Correlation**: A parameter of a joint distribution, such as the bivariate Normal
distribution, that controls how strongly two random variables change together. For a
bivariate Normal distribution, a correlation of zero means that the two variables are
independent.

- **Coverage**: The fraction of repeated hypothetical experiments for which the confidence
interval calculated with a given procedure contains the parameter. It can be checked by
simulation when the parameter that generated the samples is known.

- **Cramér–Rao bound**: A lower limit for the variance of an unbiased estimator
$\tilde\theta$: it cannot be smaller than the inverse of the Fisher information,
$\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\theta) \ge 1/\mathcal{I}(\theta)$. The information in a sample
therefore sets a limit to the precision with which a parameter can be estimated from it,
whatever the method of estimation.

- **Critical point**: A value of $x$ at which the derivative of a function is zero, so
that the function is flat there. It is a maximum when the slope changes from positive to
negative, a minimum when it changes from negative to positive, and a saddle point when the
sign of the slope does not change.

- **Cumulative probability function**: The function $F_X(x)=P(X \le x)$, the probability that
a random variable takes a value at or below $x$. It is calculated by adding probability
masses (discrete) or by integrating the density (continuous), it is always between zero and
one, and it never decreases as $x$ increases. In R, it is implemented by the `p*` functions.

- **Data-generating process**: The mechanism that produces observations in an experiment,
survey or any other relevant research protocol. It includes ecological or physical processes,
systematic relationships among variables, variation among units, measurement and sampling
procedures, and observational error. A statistical model is a simplified representation of
this process.

- **Density-scaled histogram**: A histogram in which the height of each bar is the relative
frequency of the bin divided by the width of the bin. The area of each bar equals the
relative frequency and the areas of all bars add up to one, so the histogram can be compared
with a probability density function.

- **Derivative**: The slope of a function at a point, $f'(x)=df/dx$: the change in the
output per unit change in the input, measured over an interval so short that the curve is
indistinguishable from a straight line. Its units are the units of the output divided by
those of the input. The derivative of a log-likelihood is zero at its maximum.

- **Deterministic function**: A function that assigns one output to each input for given
values of its parameters, so that the same input always gives the same output. In a model
for data it is the part that describes how the expected response changes with a predictor.

- **Discrete random variable**: A random variable that takes values from a finite or
countably infinite set, such as the counts $0, 1, 2, \ldots$. A set is **finite** when it
has a fixed maximum number of values (e.g., 0 to 4 surviving seeds out of four) and
**countably infinite** when there is no pre-specified maximum but the values can still be
listed (e.g., any non-negative integer).

- **Dispersion ratio**: The ratio of the sample variance to the sample mean. For independent
counts from a Poisson distribution it tends to be close to one, so a substantially larger
ratio suggests overdispersion. It is an exploratory diagnostic and does not identify the
cause of the extra variation.

- **Domain**: The set of values of the input $x$ for which a function is used. Many
ecological functions are used only for $x\ge0$ (a density, a size, a time).

- **Empirical cumulative distribution**: The cumulative function of the empirical
distribution: the fraction of observations at or below each value. It requires neither bins
nor a bandwidth and, for continuous data, it increases by $1/n$ at each observed value. In R,
it is calculated with `ecdf()`.

- **Empirical distribution**: The distribution represented directly by observed data, by
assuming each possible observation has a probability mass equal to its relative frequency
in the sample. It describes the observed sample in a way that we can compute quantiles and
moments, it is not a description of the data generating process.

- **Epistemic probability**: Probability interpreted as how certain we are about each
possible value when predicting an outcome, which depends on the knowledge or information
that we have about the system.

- **Estimate**: The value that an estimator returns for the sample that we actually
observed. It is marked with a hat, e.g., $\hat\lambda = 4$.

- **Estimator**: A rule (i.e., a function) that we apply to a sample to calculate a value
for a parameter. Since we treat the observations as random variables, an estimator is also
a random variable: a different sample would give a different estimate.

- **Expectation**: An operator that maps a function of a random variable to its
probability-weighted average under a specified distribution. For a function $f(X)$,

$$
E[f(X)] =
\begin{cases}
\sum_x f(x)\,P(X=x), & \text{for a discrete random variable},\\
\int f(x)f_X(x)\,dx, & \text{for a continuous random variable},
\end{cases}
$$

- **Fisher information**: A measure of how much information a sample contains about a
parameter, written $\mathcal{I}(\theta)$. The variance of a maximum likelihood estimator
approaches its inverse in large samples. From a sample we calculate the **observed
information**, minus the second derivative of the log-likelihood at the estimate,
$\hat{\mathcal{I}} = -\ell''(\hat\theta)$. A sharply curved log-likelihood has a large
information and a small variance of the estimator. With several parameters the information
is a matrix: the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood at the estimates.

- **Four faces of a distribution**: The four functions that every distribution has: the
probability mass (or density), the cumulative probability, the quantile function and the
random sampler. In R they are implemented by functions with the prefixes `d`, `p`, `q` and
`r`, followed by a short name for the distribution (e.g., `dbinom`, `pbinom`, `qbinom` and
`rbinom`).

- **Glivenko–Cantelli theorem**: The empirical cumulative distribution of an i.i.d. sample
converges uniformly (that is, for all values at once) to the cumulative distribution of the
model as the sample size grows. It extends the law of large numbers, which applies to the
relative frequency of one event at a time.

- **Half-life**: The time $t_{1/2}$ over which an exponential decay $ae^{-bt}$ falls to half
of its value, $t_{1/2}=\log 2/b$, wherever we start. It is the half-maximum idea applied to
a decline, and it is read on the time axis.

- **Half-maximum**: The value of $x$ at which a saturating function reaches half of its
asymptote. For the Michaelis–Menten function $ax/(b+x)$ it is $b$. It is read on the
horizontal axis and has the units of $x$, unlike half of the asymptote, $a/2$, which is a
value of the response.

- **Hessian**: The matrix of second derivatives of a function with respect to every pair of
its arguments. With `hessian = TRUE`, `optim()` returns the Hessian of the negative
log-likelihood at the estimates, on the scale of the parameters that were optimised. This
is the observed information matrix, and its inverse (calculated with `solve()`) approximates
the variances and covariances of the estimates.

- **Histogram**: A summary of a sample of continuous measurements. The range of the
measurements is divided into intervals (called **bins**) and the observations in each bin
are counted. Dividing each count by the sample size gives the relative frequency of the bin.
The width of the bins is a choice that changes how the same sample looks.

- **Independence**: Two random variables are independent if knowledge about one of them does
not change the probabilities for the other. Equivalently, their joint distribution is the
product of their marginal distributions, $P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2)=P(X_1=x_1)P(X_2=x_2)$ for
discrete variables and $f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)$ for continuous variables. It is a
modelling assumption: it is not guaranteed merely because observations were collected at
different locations or times.

- **Independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.)**: A set of random variables are
i.i.d. when each of them follows the same distribution and the value of one does not change
the probabilities for the others.

- **Inflection point**: A value of $x$ at which the second derivative of a function changes
sign, so that the graph changes from convex to concave or the reverse. The slope is steepest
(or shallowest) there. The midpoint $c$ of the logistic function is its inflection point.

- **Invariance**: The maximum likelihood estimate of a function of a parameter is that
function of the maximum likelihood estimate, $\widehat{g(\theta)} = g(\hat\theta)$. It allows
us to fit a model on a transformed scale (e.g., the logarithm of a positive parameter) and
to report the estimates on the original scale. Invariance carries over the estimate but not
unbiasedness.

- **Joint confidence region**: A region of the parameter space calculated so that, across
repeated hypothetical experiments, it contains the combination of parameter values that
generated the data with a given frequency. For two parameters, an approximate 95% region
contains the combinations whose relative log-likelihood is above $-3.00$ (half the 0.95
quantile of a chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom). It extends beyond the
profile likelihood interval of each parameter, because capturing two parameters at once is
more demanding than capturing one.

- **Joint distribution**: The distribution of two or more random variables together. It
assigns a probability to every combination of their values (the **product space**) or, for
continuous variables, a joint probability density function $f_{X,Y}(x,y)$ whose integral
over a region gives the probability of that region.

- **Kernel density estimate**: A smooth alternative to the histogram, calculated from a
sample without assuming a model. A small smooth curve (the kernel, by default a Normal
density) is placed on top of every observation and these curves are averaged. In R, it is
calculated with `density()`.

- **Kullback–Leibler divergence**: A measure of how far a model distribution is from the
distribution $g$ of the data generating process. For a discrete variable,
$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta) = \sum_x g(x)\log\frac{g(x)}{P(X=x\mid\theta)}.
$$
It is zero when the model assigns the right probability to every value and positive
otherwise. Maximum likelihood amounts to minimising it, so the estimator of a misspecified
model converges to the parameter values that bring the model closest to the data generating
process.

- **Kurtosis**: The fourth central moment divided by $\sigma^4$, where $\sigma$ is the
standard deviation, so it has no units. It measures how thick the tails of a
distribution are, i.e., how much of the distribution is spread far away from the mean. It is
often reported as the excess kurtosis, which subtracts 3, the kurtosis of a Normal
distribution.

- **Likelihood function**: The joint probability (or, for continuous data, the joint density)
of the observed sample, read as a function of the parameters with the data held fixed. For
i.i.d. observations,
$$
L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta).
$$
It is not a probability distribution for the parameter: it does not add up or integrate to
one over the parameter values. We use it to compare parameter values, and the value that
the data support best is the maximum likelihood estimate.

- **Likelihood slice**: The log-likelihood as a function of one parameter, with the other
parameters fixed at one value, normally their estimates. A slice needs no optimisation, but
it treats the other parameters as known, so it is narrower than the profile likelihood
unless the estimates of the parameters do not depend on each other.

- **Limit**: The value that a function approaches as its input approaches a given value,
written $\lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)$, or as $x\to\infty$ for the end behaviour. A limit can exist
even where the function itself is not defined.

- **Location parameter**: A parameter that shifts a function along the $x$ axis without
changing its shape, as $c$ does when $x$ is replaced by $x-c$. It has the units of $x$.

- **Log-likelihood**: The natural logarithm of the likelihood. For i.i.d. observations it is
a sum of log probabilities (or log densities),
$$
\ell(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta),
$$
which in R is calculated with the argument `log = TRUE` of the `d*` functions. It has its
maximum at the same parameter value as the likelihood, and it avoids numbers that are too
small for the computer to represent. Its value has no meaning by itself: only differences
between log-likelihoods calculated from the same data are meaningful.

- **Marginal distribution**: The distribution of one random variable in a joint
distribution, regardless of the value of the others. It is recovered by adding the joint
probabilities over the other variable (discrete) or by integrating the joint density over
it (continuous, which gives the **marginal density**), e.g.,
$f_Y(y)=\int f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx$.

- **Maximum likelihood estimator (MLE)**: The value of a parameter for which the likelihood
of the observed sample is highest,
$\hat\theta = \arg\max_\theta L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. The abbreviation is used for
the rule and for the value that it returns for a sample. Under regularity conditions, MLEs
are consistent, asymptotically normal and asymptotically efficient. In finite samples they
are in general biased.

- **Mean** or **Expected value**: The expectation of the random variable itself:

$$
\mu = E[X].
$$

It is the probability-weighted average value of a distribution, when it exists. For observed
data, the sample mean is the expected value of the empirical distribution, which simplifies
to the arithmetic mean:

$$
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i.
$$

- **Mean squared error (MSE)**: The expected squared distance between an estimator and the
parameter that it estimates. It combines bias and variance into one measure of the quality
of an estimator:
$$
\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta) = E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]
= \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) + \operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta)^2.
$$

- **Mechanistic function**: A function derived from assumptions about the process that
produces a pattern, so that its parameters measure something in the system, such as a rate
or a handling time. See also phenomenological function.

- **Method of moments**: A procedure to construct estimators by equating expectations of
the model distribution (the mean and central moments) to the same expectations of the
empirical distribution of the sample, and solving the resulting equations for the parameters.

- **Misspecified model**: A model that does not contain the distribution of the data
generating process, whatever the values of its parameters. The maximum likelihood estimator
then converges to the parameter values that minimise the Kullback–Leibler divergence, and
standard errors and intervals calculated as if the model had generated the data are
approximations.

- **Model**: Mathematical approximation to the data generating process. It involves at least
one distribution. Often one or more of the parameters in that distribution vary as a function
of covariates or groups, either deterministically or stochastically (with additional distributions).

- **Monotonic function**: A function that only increases or only decreases over its domain,
so that its derivative never changes sign. Exponential decay and the Michaelis–Menten
function are monotonic; the Ricker function is not.

- **Negative log-likelihood (NLL)**: Minus the log-likelihood, $-\ell(\theta)$. The function
`optim()` minimises by default, so we give it the NLL: the parameter value with the lowest
NLL is the one with the highest likelihood.

- **Nested functions**: A function is nested in another when it is the special case obtained
by fixing one of the parameters of the other at a particular value. The Michaelis–Menten
function is nested in the Hassell function, which has a third parameter $c$, and is
recovered when $c=1$. Nested functions are the usual candidates in a comparison of models.

- **Nuisance parameter**: A parameter that is needed to define the model but is not the one
that the question is about. Which parameter is of interest and which is a nuisance depends
on the question. A profile likelihood re-estimates the nuisance parameters for every value of
the parameter of interest.

- **Observation**: The value actually recorded in the real world (e.g., the number of seeds
that survived in one particular quadrat). It is written with a lower-case letter, $x$,
whereas the random variable is written $X$.

- **Overdispersion**: Variation that is greater than the variation expected under a
reference model, usually the Poisson distribution, for which the variance equals the mean.
It does not identify the ecological cause: clustering, habitat differences, omitted
predictors, detection variation and dependence among observations can all produce it. The
opposite case, a variance lower than expected, is called underdispersion.

- **Parameter**: A fixed, unknown quantity that defines a model distribution, such as the
probability $p$ of a Binomial distribution or the mean $\mu$ and standard deviation
$\sigma$ of a Normal distribution. In a deterministic function, a parameter is a constant of
the formula that stays fixed while the input varies, such as the asymptote of a
Michaelis–Menten function.

- **Partial derivative**: The derivative of a function of several variables or parameters
with respect to one of them, taken with the others held fixed, written
$\partial f/\partial a$. The partial derivative of a function with respect to a parameter
tells us how much the function moves, at a given $x$, when that parameter changes slightly.

- **Phenomenological function**: A function chosen because it has the shape of the pattern
in the data, so that its parameters describe that shape (a height, a location, a steepness)
and not a process. See also mechanistic function.

- **Plug-in estimate**: An estimate obtained by replacing an unknown parameter in a formula
by its estimate. For example, the standard error of the mean of Poisson counts,
$\sqrt{\lambda/n}$, is estimated by $\sqrt{\hat\lambda/n}$.

- **Population**: The complete set of units, events, or possible outcomes to which a
scientific question refers. In modelling, it may be a finite set of real organisms or sites,
or a conceptual population described by a probability distribution. This is not always a
useful concept, instead we will focus on the concept of data generating process.

- **Probability density function**: The function $f_X(x)$ that defines the distribution of a
continuous random variable. The probability of an interval is the integral of the density
over that interval, $P(a<X\leq b)=\int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx$, so the density is never negative and
its total area is one. A density is a probability per unit of $X$: it is not the probability
of a single value, it changes with the units of measurement, and it can be larger than one.

- **Probability distribution**: A function that assigns probabilities to every possible set
of values a random variable. For discrete random variables, it is derived through addition
from the probability mass function. For continuous variables, it is derived through
integration from the probability density function.

- **Probability mass function**: The function $P(X=x)$ that assigns a probability to every
possible value of a discrete random variable. The probabilities of all possible values add
up to one, and the probability of any set of values is obtained by adding the individual
probabilities.

- **Profile likelihood**: The maximum log-likelihood reached for each value of a parameter of
interest, when the nuisance parameters are re-estimated for every value,
$$
\ell_{\mathrm{prof}}(\theta_1) = \max_{\theta_2}\,\ell(\theta_1,\theta_2).
$$
In this course the re-estimation is done with `optim()`. A profile does not depend on how
the nuisance parameters are written, whereas a slice does.

- **Profile likelihood interval**: An approximate confidence interval that contains all the
values of a parameter whose relative profile log-likelihood is above $-1.92$ (half the 0.95
quantile of a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom). It follows from Wilks'
theorem. It does not depend on the scale of the parameter and it follows the asymmetry of
the likelihood, which is why it is the reference method of this book. Its endpoints are
found with `uniroot()`. For a model with one parameter it is simply called the likelihood
interval.

- **Pseudo-random sequence**: A sequence of numbers generated by a deterministic algorithm
and designed to have the mathematical properties needed for random sampling. It is what
the random samplers in R produce, which makes simulations reproducible.

- **Quadratic approximation**: The parabola that has the same value, slope and curvature as
a function at a chosen point $x_0$,
$f(x)\approx f(x_0)+f'(x_0)(x-x_0)+\tfrac12 f''(x_0)(x-x_0)^2$. The Wald interval of
Chapter 4 is based on the quadratic approximation of the log-likelihood at its maximum.

- **Quantile**: A value below which a specified cumulative probability lies. For data, we
calculate quantiles on the empirical distribution of the sample.

- **Quantile function**: The inverse of the cumulative probability function: given a
cumulative probability $\alpha$ it returns the value $q_\alpha$ at which that probability is
reached. For a discrete variable, $q_\alpha=\min\{x:F_X(x)\geq\alpha\}$; for a continuous
variable, $F_X(q_\alpha)=\alpha$. The median is the $0.5$ quantile. In R, it is implemented
by the `q*` functions.

- **Random variable**: A numerical quantity that can take any value within a prescribed set
(its support). It can be used to model error, variability or uncertainty. Random variables
can be discrete or continuous.

- **Range**: The set of values that the output $y$ of a function can take. Composition with
$e^{x}$ gives a range of positive values, and with the inverse logit a range between 0 and 1.

- **Relative frequency**: The number of times a value appears in a sample divided by the
sample size. For independent observations from the same distribution, it converges in
probability to the probability mass of that value as the sample size grows.

- **Relative log-likelihood**: The difference between the log-likelihood and its maximum,
$\ell(\theta)-\ell(\hat\theta)$. It is zero at the estimate and negative everywhere else,
and it shows that only differences in log-likelihood are meaningful.

- **Reparameterisation**: Writing the same function or distribution with a different set of
parameters, each of which is an expression of the old ones. The curve does not change; the
meaning, the units and the correlation of the parameters do. The Michaelis–Menten function
and the Holling type II functional response are two parameterisations of one curve.

- **Sample**: A collection of values that have been observed or simulated through a data
generating process.

- **Sampling distribution**: The distribution of the estimates of an estimator across
repeated hypothetical experiments with the same design and sample size. It is an imaginary
construct: in a real study we carry out the experiment once and never observe the sampling
distribution itself, but we can approximate it with a simulation.

- **Saturating function**: A function that increases and levels off at an upper limit
(an asymptote), as the Michaelis–Menten function does.

- **Scale parameter**: A parameter that multiplies or divides $x$ wherever $x$ appears in a
formula. Changing it stretches or compresses the curve along the $x$ axis without changing
its shape.

- **Seed**: The starting state of the algorithm that generates a pseudo-random sequence. If
the same seed is set before the same simulation, R produces the same sequence again. In R,
it is set with `set.seed()`.

- **Sigmoid function**: A function that increases slowly at first, then fast, then slowly
again, so that its graph is S-shaped, as the logistic function does.

- **Simulation**: The use of random sampling from a model with known parameters to generate
possible samples, as a way of analysing the statistical properties of a model or of an
estimation procedure.

- **Skewness**: The third central moment divided by $\sigma^3$, where $\sigma$ is the
standard deviation, so it has no units. A distribution that is symmetric around its mean
has a skewness of zero.

- **Standard deviation**: The square root of a variance. It describes the variation among
observations, which is a different quantity from the standard error.

- **Standard error (SE)**: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of an
estimator,
$$
\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta) = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)}.
$$
It describes the variation of an estimate across hypothetical experiments and has the same
units as the estimate. A larger sample reduces the standard error, but it does not reduce
the standard deviation of the observations.

- **Support**: The set of values that a random variable can take. For continuous
distributions, the support can be unconstrained (any real value), positive (any value above
zero) or constrained (any value within a range).

- **Unimodal function**: A function that rises to a single maximum and declines after it
(a hump-shaped function), as the Ricker function does.

- **Variance**: A measure of spread around the expected value, the 2nd central moment. For
data, we calculate the variance of the empirical distribution of the sample.
$$
 \operatorname{Var}(X) = E[(X-E[X])^2].
$$

- **Variance of an estimator**: The variance of its sampling distribution. For the mean of
$n$ i.i.d. observations it decreases as the sample size grows, whereas the variance of the
individual observations does not change.

- **Wald interval**: A confidence interval of the form
$\hat\theta \pm z\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)$, where $z$ is a quantile of the
standard Normal distribution (e.g., $z \approx 1.96$ for a 95% interval). It relies on the
sampling distribution of the estimator being approximately Normal, so its coverage can
differ from the confidence level in small samples. With maximum likelihood it is a quadratic
approximation of the log-likelihood around the estimate, with the standard error obtained
from the Hessian. The interval depends on the scale on which it is calculated, so for a
positive parameter it is calculated on the log scale and its endpoints are transformed back.

- **Wilks' theorem**: In large samples, twice the difference between the maximum
log-likelihood and the profile log-likelihood at the parameter value that generated the data
approximately follows a chi-squared distribution, with as many degrees of freedom as the
number of parameters that are fixed. It is the basis of profile likelihood intervals and of
joint confidence regions.

- **Zero-inflated distribution**: A mixture of two processes: with probability $p_0$ the
observation is zero (e.g., a quadrat in which no seeds arrive), and otherwise it follows
another distribution (e.g., a Poisson distribution), which can also produce zeros. For a
Poisson distribution, $P(X=0)=p_0+(1-p_0)e^{-\lambda}$, and $P(X=x)=(1-p_0)e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x/x!$
for $x>0$. See
[How to make zero-inflated distributions](distributions.qmd#sec-zero_inflated).
